reminder: A constructible number is a length that a ruler and compass build from a unit length.
definition: A [real number](c:real-number) $x$ is constructible when a segment of length $|x|$ can be built from a segment of length 1 by a finite [ruler-and-compass construction](c:ruler-and-compass-construction). Equivalently, $x$ lies in the last field of a finite chain $\mathbb{Q}=K_0\subset K_1\subset\dots\subset K_n$ of subfields of $\mathbb{R}$, where each $K_{i+1}$ is a degree 2 [field extension](c:field-extension) of $K_i$ of the form $K_i(\sqrt{a})$ with $a>0$ in $K_i$. The chain starts at the [rational numbers](c:rational-number).
examples: Every rational number is constructible, for example $3/4$.
$\sqrt{2}$ is constructible, because it is the diagonal of a unit square.
The golden ratio $(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is constructible.
Non-example: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is not constructible, because it has degree 3 over $\mathbb{Q}$ and 3 is not a power of 2.

steps: Take a constructible number $x$ with its chain of degree 2 extensions $\mathbb{Q}=K_0\subset\dots\subset K_n$.
By the tower law, the last field has degree $2^n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
So $x$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients, which means that $x$ is algebraic.
The special case adds that the degree of $x$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ divides $2^n$, so it is a power of 2.
links.why: A constructible number is always [algebraic](c:algebraic-number) of degree a power of 2, so numbers such as $\pi$ and $\sqrt[3]{2}$ cannot be constructed.

reminder: A contraction maps any two points to points that are closer by a fixed factor less than 1.
definition: A map $f\colon X\to X$ on a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is a contraction when there is a constant $k<1$ with $d(f(x),f(y))\le k\,d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$. In other words, $f$ is a [Lipschitz continuous function](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) whose constant is less than 1.
examples: The map $x\mapsto x/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a contraction with $k=1/2$.
The map $x\mapsto\cos x$ on $[0,1]$ is a contraction with $k=\sin 1$, because $|\cos'|\le\sin 1<1$ there.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ keeps every distance, so only $k=1$ works and it is not a contraction.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto 2x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ doubles distances.

steps: Take a contraction $f$ with constant $k<1$.
The inequality $d(f(x),f(y))\le k\,d(x,y)$ is the Lipschitz condition with constant $k$.
So $f$ is Lipschitz continuous, and the special case adds that a constant below 1 works.
links.why: Every contraction is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function), and the constant below 1 gives a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) on a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space).

reminder: A coset of a subgroup $H$ is a set $gH$ of all products of one element $g$ with elements of $H$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a [group](c:group) $G$. The (left) coset of an element $g\in G$ is the set $gH=\{gh : h\in H\}$, and the cosets of $H$ are the [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class) of the relation $g\sim g'$ when $g^{-1}g'\in H$. The set of all cosets is written $G/H$.
examples: In $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ with $H=3\mathbb{Z}$, the cosets are $3\mathbb{Z}$, $1+3\mathbb{Z}$ and $2+3\mathbb{Z}$.
In the symmetric group $S_3$, a subgroup of order 2 has three left cosets, and each has 2 elements.
The subgroup $H$ is itself a coset, namely $eH$ for the identity $e$.
Non-example: in $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ with $H=3\mathbb{Z}$, the set $\{0,3\}$ is not a coset, because every coset of $H$ is infinite.

steps: Define $g\sim g'$ on $G$ when $g^{-1}g'$ lies in $H$.
This relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, because $H$ contains the identity, inverses and products.
The equivalence class of $g$ is exactly the set $gH$.
So each coset is an equivalence class, and the special case is the relation that a subgroup defines.
links.why: Cosets inherit the facts about [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class): they are disjoint and they cover $G$.

reminder: The cosine of $t$ is the horizontal coordinate of the point at arc length $t$ on the unit circle.
definition: The cosine is the [function](c:function) $\cos\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ from the [real numbers](c:real-number) to themselves that gives the $x$-coordinate of the point reached by moving a distance $t$ counterclockwise along the unit circle from $(1,0)$. Equivalently, $y=\cos t$ is the solution of the [differential equation](c:differential-equation) $y''=-y$ with $y(0)=1$ and $y'(0)=0$, where $y'$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) of $y$. Its [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) is $\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n t^{2n}/(2n)!$.
examples: The cosine is even, $\cos(-t)=\cos t$, and $|\cos t|\le 1$ for all $t$.
For an acute angle in a right triangle, the cosine is the length of the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse.
Non-example: $t\mapsto 2\cos t$ also solves $y''=-y$, but $y(0)=2$, so it is not the cosine.

steps: Move along the unit circle from $(1,0)$ by a distance $t$ to reach a point $(x,y)$.
The trigonometric functions of $t$ are built from the two coordinates $x$ and $y$ of this point.
The cosine is the one that returns the first coordinate $x$.
links.why: Facts that hold for all [trigonometric functions](c:trigonometric-function), such as having period $2\pi$, apply to the cosine.

reminder: De Rham cohomology is the space of closed differential forms on a manifold modulo the exact ones.
definition: Let $M$ be a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold), and let $\Omega^k(M)$ be its space of [differential forms](c:differential-form) of degree $k$, with [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d$. The de Rham cohomology $H^k_{dR}(M)$ is the vector space of [closed](c:closed-differential-form) $k$-forms ($d\omega=0$) modulo exact $k$-forms ($\omega=d\eta$). In other words, it is the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the complex $\Omega^0\to\Omega^1\to\cdots$.
examples: For a connected manifold $M$, $H^0_{dR}(M)=\mathbb{R}$, because the closed $0$-forms are the constant functions.
$H^1_{dR}(S^1)=\mathbb{R}$, spanned by the class of the form $d\theta$.
For $k\ge1$, $H^k_{dR}(\mathbb{R}^n)=0$, which is the Poincaré lemma.
Non-example: the space of closed $1$-forms on $S^1$ is infinite-dimensional, so it is not $H^1_{dR}(S^1)$; one must divide out the exact forms.

steps: Take the complex $\Omega^0(M)\to\Omega^1(M)\to\cdots$ of differential forms with differential $d$.
Since $d\circ d=0$, this is a cochain complex of real vector spaces.
Its cohomology is the space of closed forms modulo exact forms, which is de Rham cohomology.
links.why: De Rham cohomology is one case of [cohomology](c:cohomology), so general tools such as long exact sequences apply to it.

reminder: The degree of a map counts, with signs, how many times it covers its target manifold.
definition: Let $f\colon M\to N$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) between connected [compact manifolds](c:compact-manifold) without boundary, both with an [orientation](c:orientation-of-a-manifold) and of the same dimension $n$. The degree $\deg f$ is the integer with $f_*[M]=\deg f\cdot[N]$ in $H_n(N;\mathbb{Z})$, where $[M]$ and $[N]$ are the [fundamental classes](c:fundamental-class). For smooth $f$, it is the sum of the signs of the Jacobian determinant over the points of $f^{-1}(y)$ for any regular value $y$.
examples: The identity map has degree 1, and a constant map has degree 0.
The map $z\mapsto z^k$ on the circle $S^1$ has degree $k$.
The [antipodal map](c:antipodal-map) on the sphere $S^n$ has degree $(-1)^{n+1}$.
Non-example: a map $S^1\to S^2$ has no degree, because the two manifolds have different dimensions.

steps: Take a closed curve $\gamma$ in the plane that avoids the point $0$.
Divide $\gamma(t)$ by $|\gamma(t)|$ to get a map from $S^1$ to $S^1$.
The winding number of $\gamma$ around $0$ is the degree of this map.
The degree extends this count to maps between oriented closed manifolds of any dimension $n$.
links.why: The degree is the [winding number](c:winding-number) in higher dimension, so the idea of counting turns carries over.

reminder: An integer $a$ divides an integer $b$ when $b$ equals $a$ times an integer.
definition: In a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, an element $a$ divides an element $b$, written $a\mid b$, when $b=ac$ for some $c\in R$. For the [integers](c:integer), this means that $b$ is a multiple of $a$.
examples: $3\mid 12$, because $12=3\cdot 4$.
Every integer divides $0$, and $1$ and $-1$ divide every integer.
In the Gaussian integers, $1+i$ divides $2$, because $2=(1+i)(1-i)$.
Non-example: $5$ does not divide $12$, and $0$ does not divide $3$, because $0\cdot c=0$ for every $c$.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ and write $a\mid b$ when $b=ac$ for some $c$.
Reflexivity holds, because $a=a\cdot 1$.
Transitivity holds, because $b=ac$ and $d=bc'$ give $d=a(cc')$.
So divisibility is a preorder, and on the non-negative integers it is also antisymmetric, hence a partial order.
links.why: Divisibility is a [preorder](c:is-preorder), so general facts about preorders apply to it.

reminder: The $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial is the sum of the products of all $k$-element subsets of the variables.
definition: For variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and $0\le k\le n$, the elementary symmetric [polynomial](c:polynomial) is $e_k=\sum_{1\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le n}X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$, with $e_0=1$. It is a [symmetric polynomial](c:symmetric-polynomial) of degree $k$ with one term for each $k$-element subset of the variables.
examples: For a monic polynomial $\prod_i(T-r_i)$, the coefficient of $T^{n-k}$ is $(-1)^k e_k(r_1,\dots,r_n)$, which is Vieta's formulas.
Non-example: $X_1^2+X_2^2$ is symmetric but not elementary, because $X_1^2+X_2^2=e_1^2-2e_2$.

steps: Fix $k$ and add the product of the variables over all $k$-element subsets.
A permutation of the variables sends the set of $k$-element subsets onto itself.
So the sum does not change, and $e_k$ is a symmetric polynomial.
The special case is the one whose terms are all the squarefree monomials of degree $k$, each with coefficient 1.
links.why: Each $e_k$ is [symmetric](c:symmetric-polynomial), and every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in $e_1,\dots,e_n$, so these generate all of them.

reminder: An elliptic operator is a linear differential operator whose principal symbol is invertible for every nonzero cotangent vector.
definition: Let $P$ be a [linear differential operator](c:linear-differential-operator) of order $m$ between sections of two [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) $E$ and $F$ of equal rank on a manifold $M$. Then $P$ is elliptic when its [principal symbol](c:principal-symbol) $\sigma_P(x,\xi)\colon E_x\to F_x$ is invertible for every point $x$ and every nonzero $\xi$ in the fiber of the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle) at $x$.
examples: The Laplacian $\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has symbol $-|\xi|^2$, which is nonzero for $\xi\ne0$.
The Cauchy-Riemann operator $\partial/\partial\bar z$ on the plane is elliptic.
The Dirac operator on a spin manifold is elliptic.
Non-example: the wave operator $\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2$ has symbol $\xi^2-\tau^2$ up to a sign, which vanishes when $\tau=\xi\ne0$.

steps: Take a linear differential operator $P$ of order $m$ between two vector bundles.
Replace each derivative of order $m$ in $P$ by the matching covector variable to get the principal symbol.
Ask that this symbol is invertible at every nonzero covector.
Then $P$ is elliptic, and the special case adds only this invertibility condition.
links.why: An elliptic operator is a [linear differential operator](c:linear-differential-operator) with one extra condition, and that condition gives regularity of solutions.

reminder: An embedding is a map that is an isomorphism onto its image.
definition: In a [category](c:category) of structured objects such as groups, topological spaces or smooth manifolds, a morphism $f\colon A\to B$ is an embedding when it induces an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) from $A$ onto its [image](c:image) $f(A)$, with the structure that $f(A)$ inherits from $B$. For groups this means an injective [homomorphism](c:homomorphism). For topological spaces it means a continuous injection that is a homeomorphism onto its image.
examples: The inclusion $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is an embedding of additive groups.
The inclusion of the circle $S^1$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$ is an embedding of topological spaces.
Non-example: the map $[0,2\pi)\to S^1$, $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$, is a continuous bijection but not an embedding, because its inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ with the same formula is not injective.

steps: Take a topological embedding $f\colon X\to Y$, a continuous injection that is a homeomorphism onto $f(X)$.
Homeomorphisms are the isomorphisms in the category of topological spaces.
So $f$ is an isomorphism onto its image, which is the general definition of an embedding.
links.why: Seeing a subspace inclusion as an [embedding](c:embedding) lets general facts about embeddings apply in topology.

steps: Take a smooth embedding $f\colon M\to N$, a smooth injective [immersion](c:immersion) that is a homeomorphism onto its image.
Its image is a submanifold of $N$, and $f$ is a diffeomorphism from $M$ onto this submanifold.
Diffeomorphisms are the isomorphisms of smooth manifolds, so $f$ is an isomorphism onto its image.
links.why: A smooth embedding is an isomorphism onto a submanifold, so it fits the general idea of an [embedding](c:embedding).

reminder: An ergodic map preserves a measure, and every set that it leaves invariant has zero or full measure.
definition: A map $f\colon X\to X$ on a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$ is ergodic when it is a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) and every measurable set $A$ with $f^{-1}(A)=A$, up to a null set, has $\mu(A)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus A)=0$. So $X$ cannot be split into two [invariant](c:invariant-set) pieces of positive measure.
examples: The rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha \bmod 1$ with $\alpha$ irrational is ergodic for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1)$.
The doubling map $x\mapsto 2x \bmod 1$ is ergodic for Lebesgue measure.
Non-example: the identity map on $[0,1]$ preserves Lebesgue measure, but the invariant set $[0,1/2]$ has measure $1/2$.
Non-example: the rotation $x\mapsto x+1/2 \bmod 1$ fixes the set $[0,1/4)\cup[1/2,3/4)$, which has measure $1/2$.

steps: Take a measure-preserving map $f$ of $(X,\mu)$.
Call a measurable set $A$ invariant when $f^{-1}(A)=A$ up to a null set.
Add the condition that every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure.
A measure-preserving map with this condition is ergodic.
links.why: Ergodicity is the extra condition on a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) that makes time averages equal space averages.

reminder: A Feynman diagram is a graph whose vertices and edges stand for one term in the perturbative expansion of an expectation value.
definition: Let $\mu_S$ be a [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) and let $I$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree at least 3. The [moments](c:moment) of the perturbed measure $\exp(-I)\mu_S$ are sums over [graphs](c:graph), the Feynman diagrams, in which each vertex of valence $k$ stands for a degree $k$ term of $I$, each edge stands for a factor from the covariance of $\mu_S$, and each graph carries the weight $1/|\mathrm{Aut}|$ of its symmetries.
examples: In $\varphi^4$ theory, a graph with one vertex of valence 4 and two loops, the figure eight, is a vacuum diagram.
In $\varphi^4$ theory, one vertex with a loop and two external legs is a first-order term of the two-point function.
Non-example: a graph with a vertex of valence 3 is not a diagram of pure $\varphi^4$ theory, because every vertex there has valence 4.

steps: Take a Feynman diagram, which has vertices joined by edges and possibly external legs.
Treat each external leg as an edge with a free end, and the diagram is a graph.
The special case adds the rule that a vertex of valence $k$ comes from a degree $k$ term of $I$.
It also adds a propagator on each edge and the symmetry weight $1/|\mathrm{Aut}|$ for the whole graph.
links.why: Facts about [graphs](c:graph), such as counting vertices, edges and loops, apply directly to Feynman diagrams.

reminder: A finite sum $a_1+\dots+a_n$ adds a list of finitely many terms, and the empty sum is $0$.
definition: A finite sum of terms $a_1,\dots,a_n$, such as [real numbers](c:real-number) and [integers](c:integer), is written $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ for a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$. It is defined by $\sum_{i=1}^0 a_i=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}a_i=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i+a_{n+1}$, so the order and the bracketing of the terms do not matter.
examples: $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i=n(n+1)/2$ for every $n$.
The empty sum, with no terms, equals $0$.
Non-example: $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}2^{-i}$ has infinitely many terms, so it is a [series](c:series) defined by a limit and not a finite sum.

steps: Take a finite list $a_1,\dots,a_N$ and extend it by $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$.
The partial sums of this infinite sequence equal $a_1+\dots+a_N$ for every index $n\ge N$.
So the series converges, and its value is the finite sum.
Hence a finite sum is the case of a series with only finitely many nonzero terms.
links.why: Every finite sum is a [series](c:series) with finitely many nonzero terms, so facts about series cover it.

reminder: A finite partition of $a$ is a finite set of nonzero, pairwise disjoint parts with supremum $a$.
definition: Let $a$ be an element of a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) with a least element $\bot$, such as the lattice of subsets of a set. A finite partition of $a$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) $P$ of elements different from $\bot$ such that any two different elements of $P$ are disjoint, which means that their meet is $\bot$, and such that the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) of $P$ is $a$.
examples: The singletons $\{1\},\dots,\{n\}$ form a finite partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
The set $\{a\}$ is a finite partition of $a$ when $a\ne\bot$.
Non-example: $\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ is not a finite partition of $\{1,2,3\}$, because the two parts overlap in $2$.

steps: Take a set partition $P$ of a finite set $S$ into nonempty blocks.
In the lattice of subsets of $S$, the least element is $\emptyset$, the meet is intersection and the join is union.
The blocks are nonempty, pairwise disjoint and have union $S$, so $P$ is a finite partition of the top element $S$.
A finite partition also lets $a$ be any element of a lattice with a least element, not only a set.
links.why: A [set partition](c:set-partition) of a finite set is the case of a finite partition in the lattice of subsets.

reminder: A first-order sentence is a first-order formula in which every variable is bound by a quantifier.
definition: A first-order sentence is a [formula](c:formula) of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), built from atomic formulas with connectives and the [universal quantifier](c:universal-quantifier) $\forall$ and the quantifier $\exists$, that has no free [variables](c:variable). In each [first-order structure](c:structure) it is either true or false, and no assignment of values is needed.
examples: $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x<y)$ is a sentence: it is true in $\mathbb{Z}$ and false in the finite ordered set $\{1,2,3\}$.
$\forall x\,\forall y\,(x\cdot y=y\cdot x)$ is a sentence that says a structure is commutative: it is true in $\mathbb{Z}$ and false in a non-abelian group.
$\exists x\,(x\cdot x=2)$ is a sentence that is true in $\mathbb{R}$ and false in $\mathbb{Q}$.
Non-example: $x<y$ is a formula but not a sentence, because $x$ and $y$ are free.

steps: Take a first-order formula $\varphi$ built from atomic formulas, connectives and quantifiers.
List its free variables, which are the variables that no quantifier binds.
If this list is empty, then $\varphi$ is a sentence.
Then $\varphi$ is true or false in each structure, with no assignment of values to variables.
links.why: A sentence is a [formula](c:formula) with no free variables, so it states a fact about a whole structure.

reminder: The free product of two groups is the group of alternating words in their elements with no relations between the factors.
definition: The free product $G*H$ of two [groups](c:group) $G$ and $H$ is the group of reduced words that alternate between non-identity elements of $G$ and of $H$, multiplied by joining words and then merging or cancelling neighbours from the same factor. It is the [coproduct](c:coproduct) in the category of groups: each pair of [group homomorphisms](c:group-homomorphism) $G\to K$ and $H\to K$ extends to a unique homomorphism $G*H\to K$.
examples: $\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}$ is the free group on two generators.
$\mathbb{Z}/2*\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the infinite dihedral group.

Non-example: the direct product $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ is not the free product $\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}$, because its two factors commute, while the factors of a free product satisfy no relations.

steps: In the category of groups, take two groups $G$ and $H$.
The free product comes with inclusions $G\to G*H$ and $H\to G*H$.
Any pair of homomorphisms to a group $K$ extends to a unique homomorphism $G*H\to K$.
This is the universal property of a coproduct, so $G*H$ is the coproduct of $G$ and $H$ in the category of groups.
links.why: General facts about [coproducts](c:coproduct), such as uniqueness up to isomorphism, apply to free products.

steps: Take the free group on a finite set of generators $s_1,\dots,s_n$.
It is the iterated free product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}$, one for each generator.
So every free group of finite rank is a free product of copies of $\mathbb{Z}$.
The free product allows any groups as factors, not only $\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: A [free group](c:free-group) is a free product of copies of $\mathbb{Z}$, so results on free products also describe free groups.

steps: Take an amalgamated free product $G*_AH$ of $G$ and $H$ over a common subgroup $A$.
Let $A$ be the trivial subgroup.
Then no elements are identified, so $G*_{1}H$ is the free product $G*H$.
links.why: A free product is an [amalgamated free product](c:amalgamated-product) with nothing amalgamated, so results on amalgams apply to it.

reminder: The Frobenius endomorphism of a ring of prime characteristic $p$ sends every element $x$ to $x^p$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) of prime [characteristic](c:characteristic) $p$, which means $p\cdot 1=0$ in $R$. The Frobenius endomorphism is the map $F\colon R\to R$ with $F(x)=x^p$, which is a ring [endomorphism](c:endomorphism) because $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ in $R$.
examples: On the field $\mathbb{F}_p$, the map $x\mapsto x^p$ is the identity, which is Fermat's little theorem.
On the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_p[t]$, $F(f(t))=f(t)^p=f(t^p)$.
On a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, it is an automorphism that generates the Galois group over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not additive, because $(1+1)^2=4\ne 1^2+1^2$.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ with $p\cdot 1=0$ for a prime $p$.
For $0<k<p$ the binomial coefficient $\binom{p}{k}$ is divisible by $p$, so it vanishes in $R$.
Hence $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$, and also $(xy)^p=x^py^p$ and $1^p=1$.
So $x\mapsto x^p$ is a ring homomorphism from $R$ to itself, and the special case fixes the exponent $p$.
links.why: The Frobenius map is a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism), so it respects sums and products in characteristic $p$.

reminder: A Grothendieck topos is a category equivalent to the category of sheaves of sets on a small site.
definition: A Grothendieck topos is a [category](c:category) that is equivalent to the category of [sheaves](c:sheaf) of sets on a small [Grothendieck site](c:grothendieck-site), that is, on a small category with a Grothendieck topology. Such a category has all small limits and colimits, is cartesian closed, and has a subobject classifier.
examples: The category of sets is a Grothendieck topos: it is the category of sheaves on a one-point space.
For a topological space $X$, the category $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ of sheaves on $X$ is a Grothendieck topos.
For a group $G$, the category of $G$-sets is a Grothendieck topos, the [classifying topos](c:classifying-topos) of $G$.
Non-example: the category of finite sets is not a Grothendieck topos, because it lacks infinite coproducts.

steps: Take the category of sheaves of sets on a small site.
It has finite limits, is cartesian closed and has a subobject classifier.
So it is a topos in the elementary sense.
The special case adds all small colimits and a small site that presents the category.
links.why: Every fact about a [topos](c:topos) applies to a Grothendieck topos, which adds all small colimits and a small site.

reminder: A group homomorphism is a map between groups that sends each product $ab$ to the product $f(a)f(b)$.
definition: A group homomorphism from a [group](c:group) $G$ to a group $H$ is a map $f\colon G\to H$ with $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ for all $a,b\in G$. It follows that $f$ sends the identity of $G$ to the identity of $H$ and inverses to inverses.
examples: The determinant $\det\colon GL_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}^\times$ is a group homomorphism, because $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$.
The exponential map $x\mapsto e^x$ is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb{R},+)$ to $(\mathbb{R}_{>0},\cdot)$.
Reduction modulo $n$ is a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x+1$ on $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is not a homomorphism, because it sends $0$ to $1$.

steps: A homomorphism is a map between two algebraic structures that preserves their operations.
A group has one binary operation, together with an identity and inverses.
A map that preserves the operation of a group is a group homomorphism.
Preservation of the identity and of inverses then follows from this one condition.
links.why: A group homomorphism is a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) for the structure of a group, and one condition is enough.

reminder: The halting problem asks whether a given program stops on a given input.
definition: The halting problem is the decision problem whose instances are pairs $(M,w)$ of a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$ and an input [word](c:word) $w$, and whose yes-instances are the pairs for which $M$ halts on $w$. No [algorithm](c:algorithm) decides it for all pairs, so the problem is not [decidable](c:decidability).
examples: A pair $(M,w)$ where $M$ stops at once on every input is a yes-instance.
A pair $(M,w)$ where $M$ moves right forever without writing is a no-instance.
A machine that searches for an even number greater than 2 that is not a sum of two primes halts if and only if Goldbach's conjecture is false.
Non-example: the question whether $M$ halts on $w$ within $n$ steps is not the halting problem, because one decides it by running $M$ for $n$ steps.

reminder: A harmonic form on a Riemannian manifold is a differential form that the Hodge Laplacian sends to zero.
definition: Let $M$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) and let $\Omega^k(M)$ be its [differential forms](c:differential-form) of degree $k$. With the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d$ and its adjoint $\delta$ defined by the metric, the Hodge Laplacian is $\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$, and a form $\omega$ is harmonic when $\Delta\omega=0$. On a [compact manifold](c:compact-manifold), this holds exactly when $d\omega=0$ and $\delta\omega=0$.
examples: On the flat torus $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$, the forms $dx_{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx_{i_k}$ with constant coefficients are harmonic.
On a compact connected manifold, the harmonic $0$-forms are the constant functions.
On the circle $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, the form $d\theta$ is harmonic.
Non-example: on the circle, the function $\cos\theta$ is not harmonic, because $\Delta\cos\theta=\cos\theta\ne0$.

steps: Take a function $f$ on a Riemannian manifold and view it as a $0$-form.
For a $0$-form, $\delta f=0$, so $\Delta f=\delta df$, which is the Laplace-Beltrami operator up to sign.
Hence $f$ is a harmonic function exactly when it is a harmonic $0$-form.
Harmonic forms extend this equation to forms of every degree $k$.
links.why: A harmonic form is the higher-degree version of a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function), and the same equation $\Delta u=0$ governs both.

steps: Take a differential form $\omega$ of degree $k$ on a Riemannian manifold.
Use the metric to build the adjoint $\delta$ of $d$ and the Laplacian $\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$.
Add the condition $\Delta\omega=0$, and the form is harmonic.
links.why: On a compact Riemannian manifold, every class in [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology) contains exactly one harmonic form.

reminder: The height of a prime ideal is the largest length of a chain of prime ideals that ends in it.
definition: In a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the height of a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $\mathfrak{p}$ is the supremum of the lengths $n$ of chains $\mathfrak{p}_0\subsetneq\mathfrak{p}_1\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq\mathfrak{p}_n=\mathfrak{p}$ of prime ideals. The height of an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ is the smallest height of a prime ideal that contains $I$. In number theory the same word also names the Weil height of an algebraic number, which this entry does not cover.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, the ideal $(0)$ has height $0$, and every ideal $(p)$ with $p$ prime has height $1$.
In $k[x,y]$ over a field $k$, the ideal $(x)$ has height $1$ and the ideal $(x,y)$ has height $2$.
Non-example: the quotient $k[x,y]/(x,y)\cong k$ has dimension $0$, but the height of $(x,y)$ is $2$, so height is not the dimension of the quotient.

reminder: An integer partition of $n$ writes $n$ as a sum of positive integers, and the order of the terms does not matter.
definition: A partition of a positive [integer](c:integer) $n$ is a sequence $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_k\ge1$ of positive integers with $\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_k=n$. Equivalently, it is a [multiset](c:multiset) of positive integers with sum $n$, so the order of the terms is not recorded. The number of partitions of $n$ is written $p(n)$.
examples: Every $n\ge1$ has the partition $n$ with one part and the partition $1+\dots+1$ with $n$ parts.
Non-example: $3+0+1$ is not a partition of $4$, because $0$ is not a positive integer.

steps: Take a partition $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_k$ of $n$ and forget the order of its parts.
What remains is a finite multiset of positive integers, with each part counted by its multiplicity.
Different partitions give different multisets, because sorting the multiset recovers the sequence.
The special case adds that the elements are positive and that they add up to $n$.
links.why: A partition is a [multiset](c:multiset) with a fixed sum, so counting tools for multisets apply to it.

reminder: The integral of a function over an interval is the limit of sums of its values times small widths.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f$ on an interval $[a,b]$ of the [real numbers](c:real-number), the integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is the limit of the [finite sums](c:finite-sum) $\sum_i f(t_i)\,(x_i-x_{i-1})$, where the pieces $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ of a subdivision of $[a,b]$ get smaller and $t_i$ lies in the $i$-th piece. When this limit exists, it is a number that equals the signed area between the graph of $f$ and the $x$-axis.
examples: $\int_0^1 x\,dx=\tfrac12$.
$\int_0^\pi \sin x\,dx=2$.
For a constant $c$, $\int_a^b c\,dx=c\,(b-a)$.

Non-example: the Dirichlet function, equal to $1$ on the rationals and $0$ on the irrationals, has no [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) on $[0,1]$, because every upper sum is $1$ and every lower sum is $0$.

steps: Take a function $f$ that has a Riemann integral on $[a,b]$.
Then $f$ is bounded and continuous almost everywhere, so $f$ is measurable for Lebesgue measure.
The Lebesgue integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$ equals its Riemann integral.
The Lebesgue integral also integrates functions that have no Riemann integral, such as the Dirichlet function.
links.why: Facts about the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral), such as the convergence theorems, apply to every Riemann integral.

reminder: An intersecting family is a family of sets in which every two members share at least one element.
definition: A [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $\mathcal{F}$ is intersecting when $A\cap B\ne\emptyset$ for all members $A,B\in\mathcal{F}$. Since each member meets itself, no member of an intersecting family is the empty set.
examples: All subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ that contain the element $1$ form an intersecting family.
The three $2$-element subsets of $\{1,2,3\}$ form an intersecting family.
All subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with more than $n/2$ elements form an intersecting family.
Non-example: $\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\}$ is not intersecting, because $\{1,2\}\cap\{3,4\}=\emptyset$.

steps: Take a family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ whose members are subsets of one ground set.
Test each pair $A,B$ of members for a common element.
If every pair passes the test, then $\mathcal{F}$ is an intersecting family.
So the special case adds only the condition that any two members meet.
links.why: Every intersecting family is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets), so results on families, such as counting members, apply to it.

reminder: A cardinal $\kappa$ is regular when fewer than $\kappa$ sets, each smaller than $\kappa$, have a union smaller than $\kappa$.
definition: An infinite [cardinal number](c:cardinal-number) $\kappa$ is regular when every [union](c:union) of fewer than $\kappa$ sets, each of cardinality less than $\kappa$, has cardinality less than $\kappa$. With the axiom of choice, this holds exactly when the [cofinality](c:cofinality) of $\kappa$ equals $\kappa$.
examples: $\aleph_0$ is regular, because a finite union of finite sets is finite.
$\aleph_1$ is regular, because with the axiom of choice a countable union of countable sets is countable.
With the axiom of choice, every infinite successor cardinal is regular.
Non-example: $\aleph_\omega$ is not regular, because it is the union of the countably many sets $\aleph_n$, each of smaller cardinality.

steps: Take an infinite cardinal number $\kappa$.
Compute its cofinality, the least length of a sequence of smaller ordinals that is unbounded in $\kappa$.
The cofinality never exceeds $\kappa$, and $\kappa$ is regular when the cofinality equals $\kappa$.
links.why: Regularity picks out the [cardinals](c:cardinal-number) that no shorter sequence reaches from below, which is the hypothesis of Fodor's lemma.

reminder: The Lie bracket of vector fields $X$ and $Y$ is the vector field $[X,Y]$ with $[X,Y]f=X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$.
definition: On a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, view each [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$ as a [derivation](c:derivation) $f\mapsto Xf$ of the smooth functions on $M$. The Lie bracket of $X$ and $Y$ is the vector field $[X,Y]$ with $[X,Y]f=X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$, and in coordinates $[X,Y]^i=\sum_j\bigl(X^j\partial_jY^i-Y^j\partial_jX^i\bigr)$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, $[\partial_x,\,x\partial_x]=\partial_x$.
On $\mathbb{R}^2$, the coordinate fields commute: $[\partial_x,\partial_y]=0$.
On $\mathbb{R}^2$, $[\partial_x,\,x\partial_y]=\partial_y$.
Non-example: the composite $XY$ is not a vector field in general, because it is a second-order operator, and only the difference $XY-YX$ has no second-order part.

steps: Take the vector fields on $M$ as derivations of the algebra of smooth functions.
The commutator $XY-YX$ of two derivations is again a derivation.
This bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity.
So vector fields form a Lie algebra, and $[X,Y]$ is an instance of a Lie bracket.
links.why: The bracket of vector fields is a [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket), so the vector fields on a manifold form a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).

reminder: A limit of a diagram is a cone through which every other cone over the diagram factors uniquely.
definition: Let $D\colon J\to\mathcal{C}$ be a [diagram](c:diagram) in a [category](c:category), that is, a [functor](c:functor). A [cone](c:cone) over $D$ is an object $N$ with maps $N\to D(j)$ for all objects $j$ of $J$ that commute with every map $D(f)$. A limit of $D$ is a cone $L$ such that every cone $N$ over $D$ factors through $L$ by exactly one map $N\to L$.
examples: A limit of a diagram of two objects with no maps between them is their product.
A limit of the diagram $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$ is the pullback, which in sets is $\{(x,y):f(x)=g(y)\}$.
A limit of the empty diagram is a terminal object.
Non-example: in sets, for the two-object diagram $\{A,B\}$, the set $A\times B\times\{0,1\}$ with the two projections is a cone but not a limit, because factorizations through it are not unique.

steps: Take a diagram with two objects $A$ and $B$ and no maps except identities.
A cone over it is an object $N$ with maps $N\to A$ and $N\to B$, and there is no condition to check.
A universal cone is an object $P$ with projections such that every pair of maps $N\to A$, $N\to B$ factors uniquely through $P$.
This is the product $A\times B$, so a product is a limit over a discrete diagram.
links.why: A [product](c:product) is a limit over a discrete diagram, so facts proved for all limits hold for products.

steps: Take the diagram $X\xrightarrow{f}Z\xleftarrow{g}Y$ with three objects and two maps.
A cone over it is an object $N$ with maps $a\colon N\to X$ and $b\colon N\to Y$ such that $fa=gb$.
The limit is the universal such cone, which is the pullback of $f$ and $g$.
links.why: A [pullback](c:pullback) is a limit over a cospan, so facts proved for all limits hold for pullbacks.

steps: Take the diagram of two parallel maps $f,g\colon X\to Y$.
A cone over it is a map $e\colon N\to X$ with $fe=ge$.
The limit is the universal such map, which is the equalizer of $f$ and $g$.
links.why: An [equalizer](c:equalizer) is a limit over two parallel maps, so facts proved for all limits hold for equalizers.

reminder: A line integral adds up the values of a function or a $1$-form along a curve.
definition: Let $\gamma\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth [curve](c:curve). For a function $f$, the line integral is $\int_\gamma f\,ds=\int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\,|\gamma'(t)|\,dt$, and for a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $1$, it is $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_a^b\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))\,dt$. Both are ordinary [integrals](c:integral) over the parameter interval.
examples: With $f=1$, the line integral over $\gamma$ is the length of the curve.
For $\omega=d\theta$ on the unit circle traversed once counterclockwise, $\int_\gamma d\theta=2\pi$.
For $\omega=dx$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,0)$, the line integral is $1$.
Non-example: the area integral $\iint_D f\,dA$ over a disk $D$ is not a line integral, because $D$ is a region and not a curve.

steps: Take the curve $\gamma(t)=t$ for $a\le t\le b$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
Then $|\gamma'(t)|=1$, so the line integral of $f$ is $\int_a^b f(t)\,dt$.
So the ordinary integral over an interval is the line integral along a straight segment.
A general line integral replaces the interval by a curve in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: A line integral is the [integral](c:integral) of one variable carried along a curve, so its rules for sums and limits carry over.

steps: Take a smooth curve $\gamma\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ as an oriented $1$-dimensional domain.
Integration of differential forms integrates a $k$-form over an oriented $k$-dimensional domain.
For $k=1$, pull the $1$-form $\omega$ back along $\gamma$ to get $\gamma^*\omega=g(t)\,dt$ on $[a,b]$.
Then $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_a^b g(t)\,dt$, so the line integral of a $1$-form is the case $k=1$.
links.why: The line integral of a $1$-form is the case $k=1$ of [integration of differential forms](c:integration-of-differential-forms), so Stokes-type theorems apply.

reminder: A Lipschitz function changes its output by at most a fixed multiple of the change in its input.
definition: A function $f\colon X\to Y$ between [metric spaces](c:metric-space) is Lipschitz when there is a constant $K\ge0$ with $d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le K\,d_X(x,x')$ for all $x,x'\in X$. The least such $K$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$.
examples: The function $|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz with constant $1$.
The function $\sin$ is Lipschitz with constant $1$, because $|\cos|\le1$.
Every differentiable function on an interval with bounded derivative is Lipschitz, by the mean value theorem.
Non-example: $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$ is not Lipschitz, because its slope near $0$ is unbounded.

steps: Take a contraction $f\colon X\to X$ on a metric space, with constant $k<1$.
The inequality $d(f(x),f(y))\le k\,d(x,y)$ is the Lipschitz condition with $K=k$.
So every contraction is a Lipschitz function, and a Lipschitz function allows any constant $K$, not only $K<1$.
links.why: A [contraction](c:contraction-mapping) is a Lipschitz function with constant below $1$, so Lipschitz functions are the wider family.

steps: Take a Lipschitz function $f$ with constant $K>0$ and a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$.
Choose $\delta=\varepsilon/K$, which does not depend on the point.
If $d(x,x')<\delta$, then $d(f(x),f(x'))\le K\,d(x,x')<\varepsilon$.
So $f$ is uniformly continuous, and the Lipschitz condition adds a linear bound between $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$.
links.why: A Lipschitz function is [uniformly continuous](c:uniform-continuity), with $\delta$ proportional to $\varepsilon$.

reminder: A local extremum of a function is a point whose value is the largest or smallest among all nearby values.
definition: Let $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ be a [function](c:function) on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. A point $a\in X$ is a local maximum when $f(x)\le f(a)$ for all $x$ in some [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $a$, and a local minimum when $f(x)\ge f(a)$ for all such $x$. A local extremum is a local maximum or a local minimum.
examples: $f(x)=x^2$ has a local minimum at $0$.
$f(x)=x^3-3x$ has a local maximum at $x=-1$ and a local minimum at $x=1$.
$\sin x$ has a local maximum at every point $\pi/2+2\pi k$.
Non-example: $f(x)=x^3$ has $f'(0)=0$, but $0$ is not a local extremum, because $f$ is negative to the left of $0$ and positive to the right.

reminder: A local system is a sheaf on a space that looks like a constant sheaf near each point.
definition: A local system on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\mathcal{L}$ of abelian groups or vector spaces that is [locally constant](c:locally-constant-sheaf): each point has an open neighborhood $U$ such that $\mathcal{L}|_U$ is isomorphic to a [constant sheaf](c:constant-sheaf). On a connected and sufficiently nice space, a local system is the same as a representation of the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group), given by parallel transport along loops.
examples: The constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ on any space $X$ is a local system.
On the circle $S^1$, the real local system of rank $1$ with monodromy $-1$ around the circle has stalks $\mathbb{R}$ and no nonzero global sections.
The sheaf of local solutions of $y'=y/(2z)$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is a local system of rank $1$ with monodromy $-1$.
Non-example: a skyscraper sheaf at a point of $\mathbb{R}$ is not a local system, because its stalks are zero away from the point and nonzero at it.

steps: Take a sheaf $\mathcal{L}$ of abelian groups on a space $X$.
For each point, look for an open neighborhood $U$ where $\mathcal{L}|_U$ is isomorphic to a constant sheaf.
If every point has such a neighborhood, then $\mathcal{L}$ is locally constant.
A locally constant sheaf of abelian groups is a local system, so the special case adds local constancy.
links.why: A local system is a [sheaf](c:sheaf), so sheaf cohomology and other sheaf tools apply, and local constancy adds monodromy.

steps: Take the constant sheaf $\underline{A}$ with value an abelian group $A$ on a space $X$.
Choose $U=X$ as the neighborhood of every point.
Then $\underline{A}|_U$ is a constant sheaf, so $\underline{A}$ is locally constant.
A local system also allows twisting around loops, which a constant sheaf never does.
links.why: A [constant sheaf](c:constant-sheaf) is the local system with trivial monodromy, so local systems are the wider family.

reminder: A locally compact group is a topological group whose underlying space is locally compact and Hausdorff.
definition: A locally compact group is a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$ whose underlying space is [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) and [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space), which means that each point has a compact neighborhood. Such a group carries a left-invariant [Haar measure](c:haar-measure).
examples: The groups $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ are locally compact groups.
Every discrete group is locally compact, and so is every compact group such as $S^1$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ with the usual topology and addition is not locally compact, because no neighborhood of $0$ has compact closure.
Non-example: an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space under addition is not locally compact, because its closed unit ball is not compact.

steps: Take a topological group $G$, a group with a topology for which multiplication and inversion are continuous.
Ask that $G$ is Hausdorff.
Ask also that the identity has a compact neighborhood.
Translations are homeomorphisms, so every point then has a compact neighborhood and $G$ is locally compact.
links.why: A locally compact group is a [topological group](c:topological-group) with one local condition, and that condition gives a Haar measure.

steps: Take a compact group $G$, a topological group whose space is compact and Hausdorff.
The whole space $G$ is a compact neighborhood of each of its points.
So $G$ is locally compact and Hausdorff.
Locally compact groups also include noncompact groups, such as $\mathbb{R}^n$ and infinite discrete groups.
links.why: Every [compact group](c:compact-group) is locally compact, so results on locally compact groups cover compact ones.

reminder: The loop space of a pointed space is the space of loops that start and end at the base point.
definition: Let $(X,x_0)$ be a [pointed topological space](c:pointed-topological-space). The loop space $\Omega X$ is the set of continuous maps $\gamma\colon[0,1]\to X$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x_0$, with the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology). It is a pointed space whose base point is the constant loop at $x_0$.
examples: For the circle $S^1$, the loop space $\Omega S^1$ is homotopy equivalent to the discrete space $\mathbb{Z}$.
For every $n\ge0$, the [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_n(\Omega X)$ is isomorphic to $\pi_{n+1}(X)$.
Non-example: the [free loop space](c:free-loop-space) $LX$ of all continuous maps $S^1\to X$ is not the loop space, because its loops may start at any point.

steps: Define the iterated loop space $\Omega^nX$ as the space of based maps from the sphere $S^n$ to $X$.
For $n=1$, a based map $S^1\to X$ is a loop in $X$ that starts and ends at $x_0$.
So $\Omega^1X$ is exactly the loop space $\Omega X$.
Repeating the loop construction gives $\Omega^{n+1}X=\Omega(\Omega^nX)$ for every $n\ge1$.
links.why: The loop space is the first step of the [iterated loop spaces](c:iterated-loop-space) $\Omega^nX$, which describe higher homotopy.

reminder: The Mahler measure of a polynomial is $|a|\prod\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$, with $a$ the leading coefficient and $\alpha_i$ the roots.
definition: Let $P(x)=a\prod_{i=1}^{d}(x-\alpha_i)$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with complex coefficients, leading coefficient $a\ne0$ and [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$. Its Mahler measure is $M(P)=|a|\prod_{i=1}^{d}\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$, so only the roots outside the unit circle contribute, through their [absolute value](c:absolute-value).
examples: $M(x-2)=2$, because the only root has absolute value $2$.
$M(x^2-x-1)=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$, because the roots are $\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ and only the first has absolute value above $1$.
$M(2x-1)=2$, because $|a|=2$ and the root $1/2$ lies inside the unit circle.
Non-example: the product of the absolute values of all roots of $x-\tfrac12$ is $\tfrac12$, but $M(x-\tfrac12)=1$, because roots inside the unit circle count as $1$.

reminder: A Markov kernel assigns to each point of a space a probability measure on a second space, varying measurably with the point.
definition: A Markov kernel from a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\mathcal{A})$ to a measurable space $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ is a map $\kappa$ that gives each $x\in X$ a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\kappa(x,\cdot)$ on $Y$, such that $x\mapsto\kappa(x,B)$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) for every $B\in\mathcal{B}$. It models a random choice of a point in $Y$ that depends on $x$.
examples: The transition matrix $(p_{ij})$ of a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) on a finite set is a Markov kernel with $\kappa(i,\{j\})=p_{ij}$.
The map $x\mapsto N(x,1)$, which sends $x$ to the normal distribution with mean $x$ and variance $1$, is a Markov kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
Every measurable map $f$ gives the kernel $x\mapsto\delta_{f(x)}$, where $\delta$ is the Dirac measure.
Non-example: the rule $\kappa(x,\cdot)=$ Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ for every $x$ is not a Markov kernel, because its total mass is infinite and not $1$.

steps: Take a measurable function $f\colon X\to Y$.
Send each $x$ to the Dirac measure $\delta_{f(x)}$ at the point $f(x)$.
The value $\delta_{f(x)}(B)$ is the indicator of the measurable set $f^{-1}(B)$ at $x$, so it is measurable in $x$.
So this is a Markov kernel, and general kernels also allow random outputs, which a function cannot give.
links.why: A Markov kernel is a function with random output, and a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) is the case where the output is certain.

reminder: The moment generating function of a random variable $X$ is the function $t\mapsto E[e^{tX}]$.
definition: For a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$, the moment generating function is $M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}]$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the [exponential](c:exponential-function) of $tX$, defined for the real $t$ where this expectation is finite. If it is finite on an open interval around $0$, then $M_X^{(n)}(0)=E[X^n]$ for all $n$, so its derivatives at $0$ are the [moments](c:moment) of $X$.
examples: For a Bernoulli variable with $P(X=1)=p$, $M_X(t)=1-p+pe^t$.
For a standard normal variable, $M_X(t)=e^{t^2/2}$.
For a fair sign $X=\pm1$, $M_X(t)=\cosh t$.
Non-example: for a Cauchy variable, $E[e^{tX}]=\infty$ for every $t\ne0$, so there is no moment generating function near $0$.

steps: Take the law $\mu$ of $X$, a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$.
Its two-sided Laplace transform is $s\mapsto\int e^{-sx}\,d\mu(x)$.
At $s=-t$, this integral equals $E[e^{tX}]$.
So $M_X(t)$ is the Laplace transform of the law of $X$, evaluated at $-t$.
links.why: The moment generating function is a [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) of a law, so facts such as uniqueness and analyticity carry over.

reminder: A Nash equilibrium is a choice of strategy for each player such that no player gains by changing alone.
definition: In a game with players $1,\dots,n$, a profile of strategies $(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ is a Nash equilibrium when each $s_i$ is a best reply to the others: no player $i$ gets a higher payoff by changing $s_i$ while the other players keep their strategies. The strategies can be pure or [mixed](c:mixed-strategy), and every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies.
examples: In the prisoner's dilemma, the pair (defect, defect) is the only Nash equilibrium.
In matching pennies, the only equilibrium has each player choose heads with probability $1/2$.
In a coordination game where both players gain only by choosing the same side, both (left, left) and (right, right) are Nash equilibria.
Non-example: in the prisoner's dilemma, the pair (cooperate, cooperate) is not an equilibrium, because each player gains by defecting alone.

reminder: A nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a vector space satisfies $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$.
definition: A [linear map](c:linear-map) $N\colon V\to V$ from a [vector space](c:vector-space) to itself, that is, an [endomorphism](c:endomorphism) of $V$, is nilpotent when $N^k=N\circ\dots\circ N=0$ for some integer $k\ge1$. The least such $k$ is the index of nilpotency, and it is at most $\dim V$ when $V$ is finite-dimensional.
examples: A strictly upper triangular matrix, such as $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, is nilpotent.
Differentiation $d/dx$ on the polynomials of degree at most $n$ is nilpotent, because $(d/dx)^{n+1}=0$.
The zero map is nilpotent with $k=1$.
Non-example: a nonzero projection $P$ with $P^2=P$ is not nilpotent, because $P^k=P\ne0$ for all $k$.

steps: The endomorphisms of $V$ form a ring, with sum and composition as the operations.
In a ring, an element $x$ is nilpotent when $x^k=0$ for some $k\ge1$.
Here $x^k$ is the $k$-fold composition $N^k$, and $0$ is the zero map.
So the nilpotent endomorphisms of $V$ are exactly the nilpotent elements of this ring.
links.why: General facts about [nilpotent elements](c:nilpotent-element), such as the invertibility of $1-x$, apply to nilpotent endomorphisms.

reminder: A Noetherian module is a module in which every ascending chain of submodules becomes constant.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$ is Noetherian when it satisfies the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition) on [submodules](c:submodule): every chain $M_1\subseteq M_2\subseteq\cdots$ of submodules of $M$ is eventually constant. Equivalently, every submodule of $M$ is finitely generated.
examples: Every finite-dimensional vector space is a Noetherian module over its field.
$\mathbb{Z}^n$ is a Noetherian module over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Every finitely generated module over a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) is Noetherian.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a Noetherian $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because the chain $\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq\frac12\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq\frac14\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq\cdots$ never stops.

steps: Take a module $M$ over a ring $R$.
Look at the ascending chains of submodules of $M$.
If every such chain is eventually constant, then $M$ is Noetherian, and the special case adds exactly this condition.
links.why: A Noetherian module is a [module](c:module) with a finiteness condition that makes every submodule finitely generated.

steps: Take a ring $R$ and view it as a module over itself.
The submodules of $R$ are exactly its ideals.
So $R$ is a Noetherian ring if and only if $R$ is a Noetherian module over itself.
The module notion applies to every module, not only to the ring itself.
links.why: A [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) is a ring that is a Noetherian module over itself, so the module notion is the wider one.

reminder: A term is in normal form when no rewrite rule applies to it.
definition: Let a [rewriting system](c:rewriting-system) be given, with a set of terms and a rewrite relation $t\to t'$. A term $t$ is in normal form when no $t'$ satisfies $t\to t'$, so $t$ admits no further rewrite step. A normal form of a term $s$ is a term in normal form that finitely many rewrite steps reach from $s$.
examples: In arithmetic with rules such as $2+3\to5$, the numeral $5$ is in normal form.
For the single rule $x\cdot1\to x$, the term $y$ is in normal form.
In the lambda calculus, $\lambda x.x$ is in normal form.
Non-example: $(\lambda x.x)\,y$ is not in normal form, because [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction) rewrites it to $y$.

reminder: NP is the class of decision problems whose yes-answers have certificates that a computer checks in polynomial time.
definition: NP is the [complexity class](c:complexity-class) of languages $L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$, that is, decision problems, for which there are a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier $V$ such that $x\in L$ if and only if some certificate $w$ with $|w|\le p(|x|)$ makes $V(x,w)$ accept. Equivalently, a nondeterministic [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) decides $L$ in polynomial time.
examples: Boolean satisfiability is in NP: a satisfying assignment is a certificate that a computer checks in polynomial time.
The set of composite numbers is in NP: a nontrivial factor is a certificate.
Every problem solvable in polynomial time is in NP, with an empty certificate.
Non-example: the [halting problem](c:halting-problem) is not in NP, because no algorithm decides it at all.

steps: A complexity class is a set of decision problems defined by a resource bound on a machine model.
Choose the Turing machine as the model and polynomial time as the bound.
Allow nondeterminism, or equivalently a certificate that a deterministic machine checks.
The set of languages that meet this bound is NP.
links.why: NP is one [complexity class](c:complexity-class), the one defined by polynomial-time verification of certificates.

reminder: An ordered ring is a ring with a total order that respects addition and keeps products of non-negative elements non-negative.
definition: An ordered ring is a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with a [total order](c:total-order) $\le$ such that $a\le b$ implies $a+c\le b+c$ for all $c$, and $0\le a$ and $0\le b$ imply $0\le ab$. In such a ring every square is non-negative.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$, the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ and the reals $\mathbb{R}$ with their usual orders are ordered rings.
The subring $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is an ordered ring with the order from $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the complex numbers have no total order that makes them an ordered ring, because $i^2=-1$ would have to be non-negative.

steps: Take an ordered field $F$, a field with a total order that respects addition and products of non-negative elements.
Every field is a ring, so $F$ is a ring.
The order axioms of $F$ are exactly those of an ordered ring.
So every ordered field is an ordered ring, and ordered rings need not have inverses.
links.why: Every [ordered field](c:ordered-field) is an ordered ring, so facts about ordered rings apply to $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Take a ring $R$ and a total order $\le$ on its elements.
Require that $a\le b$ gives $a+c\le b+c$ for all $a,b,c$.
Require that $0\le a$ and $0\le b$ give $0\le ab$.
A ring with such an order is an ordered ring.
links.why: An ordered ring is a [ring](c:ring) with a compatible order, so every ring fact still holds for it.

reminder: An ordinal is the order type of a well-ordered set.
definition: Two [well-ordered](c:is-well-order) sets have the same order type when an order-preserving bijection joins them, and an ordinal is such an order type. In von Neumann's model, an ordinal is a [set](c:set) that is transitive and well-ordered by membership, so each ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals.
examples: The finite ordinals are $0=\emptyset$, $1=\{0\}$, $2=\{0,1\}$ and so on, and $\omega$ is the order type of $\mathbb{N}$.
$\omega+1$ is the order type of $\mathbb{N}$ with one new largest element, and it differs from $\omega$ because it has a greatest element.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ with its usual order is not well-ordered, because it has no least element, so it has no order type among the ordinals.

steps: Take a natural number $n$ and view it as the set $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$.
This set is well-ordered by its usual order, so its order type is an ordinal.
Different natural numbers give different ordinals, so the natural numbers are the finite ordinals.
Ordinals continue beyond all natural numbers, and $\omega$ is the first ordinal after them.
links.why: Ordinals extend counting beyond the [natural numbers](c:natural-number), so induction and recursion extend with them.

reminder: The partition function of a system sums the Boltzmann weights $e^{-\beta E}$ over all its states.
definition: For a system with states $s$ and energies $E(s)$ at inverse temperature $\beta$, the partition function is $Z(\beta)=\sum_s e^{-\beta E(s)}$, with an integral in place of the sum for continuous states. In quantum mechanics it is the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) $Z(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}$ of the Hamiltonian $H$, and in field theory it is a [path integral](c:path-integral). The [Boltzmann distribution](c:boltzmann-distribution) gives the state $s$ the probability $e^{-\beta E(s)}/Z(\beta)$.
examples: A two-level system with energies $0$ and $\varepsilon$ has $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$.
The harmonic oscillator with frequency $\omega$ has $Z=\dfrac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}}$.
Non-example: the probability $e^{-\beta E(s)}/Z$ of one state is not the partition function, because it is one weight divided by the partition function.

reminder: A perfect matching of a graph is a set of edges such that every vertex lies on exactly one of them.
definition: A perfect matching of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a [matching](c:matching) of $G$, a set of pairwise disjoint [edges](c:edge), that covers every [vertex](c:vertex) of $G$. So every vertex lies on exactly one edge of the matching.
examples: The $4$-cycle $abcd$ has two perfect matchings: $\{ab,cd\}$ and $\{bc,da\}$.
In the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$, each bijection between the two sides gives a perfect matching.
Non-example: a path with $3$ vertices has no perfect matching, because a perfect matching needs an even number of vertices.
Non-example: in the path $a-b-c-d$, the single edge $bc$ is a matching but not a perfect matching, because $a$ and $d$ stay uncovered.

steps: Take a matching $M$ of $G$, a set of edges no two of which share a vertex.
Count the vertices that no edge of $M$ touches.
If this count is zero, then $M$ covers every vertex.
So the special case adds that the matching covers all vertices, and then $|M|=|V|/2$.
links.why: Every perfect matching is a [matching](c:matching), so facts about matchings apply, and the extra condition forces $|V|$ to be even.

reminder: A word has period $p$ when each of its letters equals the letter $p$ places later.
definition: Let $w=w_1w_2\cdots w_n$ be a [word](c:word) of length $n$ over some alphabet. An [integer](c:integer) $p$ with $1\le p\le n$ is a period of $w$ when $w_i=w_{i+p}$ for all $i$ with $1\le i\le n-p$. The period of $w$ is its smallest period.
examples: The word $abaababa$ has the periods $5$, $7$ and $8$.
The word $aaaa$ has the periods $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$.
Every word of length $n$ has period $n$, because the condition is empty.
Non-example: $1$ is not a period of $aab$, because $w_2=a$ differs from $w_3=b$.

reminder: A perverse sheaf is a constructible complex of sheaves whose support dimensions satisfy a degree bound, and so do those of its dual.
definition: Let $X$ be a complex algebraic variety. A perverse sheaf on $X$ is an object $P$ of the bounded [derived category](c:derived-category) $D^b_c(X)$ of [constructible sheaves](c:constructible-sheaf) such that $\dim\operatorname{supp}\mathcal{H}^{-i}(P)\le i$ for all $i$, which is the support condition, and the Verdier dual $\mathbb{D}P$ satisfies the same inequalities, which is the cosupport condition. These objects form the heart of the perverse $t$-structure, which is an abelian category.
examples: On a smooth variety $X$ of dimension $n$, the shifted constant sheaf $\mathbb{C}_X[n]$ is a perverse sheaf.
A skyscraper sheaf at a point is a perverse sheaf.
The intersection complex of an irreducible subvariety is a perverse sheaf.
Non-example: the constant sheaf $\mathbb{C}_X$ in degree $0$ on a smooth variety of dimension $n>0$ is not perverse, because $\dim\operatorname{supp}\mathcal{H}^0=n>0$.

steps: Take a local system $L$ of finite rank on a smooth complex variety $X$ of dimension $n$.
Shift it to the complex $L[n]$, which has $L$ in degree $-n$ only.
Its one cohomology sheaf has support of dimension $n$ in degree $-n$, so the support condition holds.
Its Verdier dual is $L^\vee[n]$, a shifted local system, so the cosupport condition holds and $L[n]$ is perverse.
links.why: Perverse sheaves contain shifted [local systems](c:local-system) as special cases and also handle singular spaces and singular supports.

reminder: A pre-measure is a countably additive, non-negative set function on an algebra of sets that is zero on the empty set.
definition: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an [algebra of sets](c:algebra-of-sets) on a set $X$. A pre-measure on $\mathcal{A}$ is a function $\mu_0\colon\mathcal{A}\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu_0(\emptyset)=0$ that is countably additive: if $A_1,A_2,\dots$ are disjoint sets of $\mathcal{A}$ whose union $A$ also lies in $\mathcal{A}$, then $\mu_0(A)=\sum_n\mu_0(A_n)$. Every pre-measure extends to a [measure](c:measure) on the generated [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra), and the extension is unique when the pre-measure is $\sigma$-finite.
examples: The length of finite disjoint unions of half-open intervals $[a,b)$ is a pre-measure on the algebra that they generate, and it extends to Lebesgue measure.
Every measure, restricted to an algebra of sets, is a pre-measure.

Non-example: on the algebra of finite and cofinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, set $\mu(A)=0$ for finite $A$ and $\mu(A)=1$ for cofinite $A$. This is finitely additive but not a pre-measure, because $\mathbb{N}$ is a disjoint union of singletons of measure $0$, while $\mu(\mathbb{N})=1$.

steps: Take a measure $\mu$ on a sigma-algebra $\Sigma$ of subsets of $X$.
A sigma-algebra is closed under complements and finite unions, so $\Sigma$ is an algebra of sets.
The measure satisfies $\mu(\emptyset)=0$ and countable additivity on all of $\Sigma$, so it satisfies them on $\Sigma$ viewed as an algebra.
So $\mu$ is a pre-measure, and a general pre-measure is defined on a smaller family of sets.
links.why: A pre-measure is a [measure](c:measure) that lives on an algebra only, and Carathéodory's theorem turns it into a full measure.

reminder: A pullback of two maps into $Z$ is a universal square: an object with maps to the sources that agree in $Z$.
definition: Given maps $f\colon X\to Z$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ in a [category](c:category), a pullback is an object $P$ with maps $p\colon P\to X$ and $q\colon P\to Y$ such that $fp=gq$, and such that every pair $a\colon N\to X$, $b\colon N\to Y$ with $fa=gb$ factors as $a=pu$, $b=qu$ through a unique $u\colon N\to P$. It is the [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of the diagram $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$.
examples: In sets, the pullback of $f$ and $g$ is $\{(x,y)\in X\times Y: f(x)=g(y)\}$.
For two subsets $A,B\subseteq Z$ with their inclusions, the pullback is the intersection $A\cap B$.
For $f\colon X\to Z$ and a point $z\in Z$, the pullback of $f$ and $\{z\}\hookrightarrow Z$ is the fiber $f^{-1}(z)$.
Non-example: for $f=g=\mathrm{id}$ on $\{0,1\}$, the product $\{0,1\}^2$ with its two projections is not a pullback, because $fp\ne gq$; the pullback is the diagonal.

steps: Take the diagram $X\xrightarrow{f}Z\xleftarrow{g}Y$, a functor from a category with three objects.
A cone over it is an object $N$ with maps $a\colon N\to X$ and $b\colon N\to Y$ such that $fa=gb$.
The map $N\to Z$ is determined by $a$ and $b$, so the cones are the commuting squares.
The limit is the universal such cone, and this is the pullback.
links.why: A pullback is a [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of a cospan, so facts proved for all limits hold for pullbacks.
